claim: Recent experiments have produced several Anopheles gambiae homing gene drives that disrupt female fertility genes.
source: Recent experiments have produced several Anopheles gambiae homing gene drives that disrupt female fertility genes, thereby eventually inducing population collapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work on Anopheles gene drives.

claim: Homing gene drives that disrupt female fertility genes can eventually induce population collapse.
source: Recent experiments have produced several Anopheles gambiae homing gene drives that disrupt female fertility genes, thereby eventually inducing population collapse.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results cited in the manuscript.

claim: Homing gene drives may be highly effective tools to combat malaria.
source: Such drives may be highly effective tools to combat malaria.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential application of gene drives.

claim: A homing drive based on the zpg promoter driving CRISPR/Cas9 was able to eliminate a cage population of mosquitoes.
source: One such homing drive, based on the zpg promoter driving CRISPR/Cas9, was able to eliminate a cage population of mosquitoes.
evidence: This refers to experimental results from previous studies.

claim: A second version of the zpg drive incorporating an X-shredder element was similarly successful at eliminating cage populations.
source: A second version, purportedly improved upon the first by incorporating an X-shredder element (which biases inheritance towards male offspring), was similarly successful.
evidence: This refers to experimental results from previous studies.

claim: X-shredder elements bias inheritance towards male offspring.
source: A second version, purportedly improved upon the first by incorporating an X-shredder element (which biases inheritance towards male offspring), was similarly successful.
evidence: This is established knowledge about X-shredder mechanisms.

claim: The combined homing/X-shredder drive is less effective at population suppression within the context of the mosquito population model.
source: We find that the combined homing/X-shredder drive is actually less effective at population suppression within the context of our mosquito population model.
evidence: This is based on simulation results presented in the study.

claim: The combined homing/X-shredder drive often fails to completely suppress the population, instead resulting in an unstable equilibrium between drive and wild-type alleles.
source: In particular, the combined drive often fails to completely suppress the population, instead resulting in an unstable equilibrium between drive and wild-type alleles.
evidence: This is based on simulation results presented in the study.

claim: Drives based on the nos promoter may prove to be more promising candidates for future development than originally thought.
source: By contrast, otherwise similar drives based on the nos promoter may prove to be more promising candidates for future development than originally thought.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and inference from the data.

claim: Malaria kills over 400,000 people every year.
source: Because malaria kills over 400,000 people every year while infecting over 200 million (World Health Organization, 2019), even a modest increase in the efficiency of a gene drive could correspond to a substantial decrease in new cases per year.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization.

claim: Malaria infects over 200 million people every year.
source: Because malaria kills over 400,000 people every year while infecting over 200 million (World Health Organization, 2019), even a modest increase in the efficiency of a gene drive could correspond to a substantial decrease in new cases per year.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization.

claim: A modest increase in the efficiency of a gene drive could correspond to a substantial decrease in new malaria cases per year.
source: Because malaria kills over 400,000 people every year while infecting over 200 million (World Health Organization, 2019), even a modest increase in the efficiency of a gene drive could correspond to a substantial decrease in new cases per year.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high disease burden.

claim: Several population suppression drives targeting female fertility genes have recently proven successful in laboratory settings.
source: Malaria reduction strategies based on gene drives (Wang et al., 2022; Hay et al., 2021; Quinn and Nolan, 2020; Dhole et al., 2020) in Anopheles mosquitoes have made substantial advances (Simoni et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018; Adolfi et al., 2020; Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020), with several population suppression drives targeting female fertility genes recently proving successful in laboratory settings (Simoni et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: If a homing suppression drive targeting a female fertility gene can avoid the development of resistance alleles that preserve the function of the gene, it can eliminate or at least reduce the population.
source: Initial modeling studies assuming a panmictic population indicated that if a homing suppression drive targeting a female fertility gene can avoid the development of resistance alleles that preserve the function of the gene, it can eliminate or at least reduce the population.
evidence: This is based on previous modeling studies.

claim: The exact level of suppression is a function of both species-specific ecological factors and the suppressive power of the drive.
source: The exact level of suppression is a function of both species-specific ecological factors and the suppressive power of the drive.
evidence: This is based on established modeling knowledge.

claim: Genetic load for Anopheles female-fertility homing drives is typically defined as the fractional reduction in average fertility of a population in which the drive has reached its equilibrium frequency as compared to an otherwise identical wild-type population.
source: Suppressive power is often characterized in terms of the drive's 'genetic load', which for Anopheles female-fertility homing drives is typically defined as the fractional reduction in average fertility of a population in which the drive has reached its equilibrium frequency as compared to an otherwise identical wild-type population.
evidence: This is a definition based on established modeling conventions.

claim: If the genetic load is high enough, panmictic models predict complete population elimination.
source: In general, if the genetic load is high enough, panmictic models predict complete population elimination, and any increase in genetic load beyond that threshold can at most provide a decrease in the time to elimination (Deredec et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Any increase in genetic load beyond the elimination threshold can at most provide a decrease in the time to elimination in panmictic models.
source: In general, if the genetic load is high enough, panmictic models predict complete population elimination, and any increase in genetic load beyond that threshold can at most provide a decrease in the time to elimination (Deredec et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Population structure can substantially delay or prevent complete population suppression even by drives with a sufficient genetic load to reliably induce population collapse in a panmictic population.
source: However, spatially explicit models have indicated that outcomes of a suppression drive release can be substantially more complicated than those predicted by panmictic population models. In particular, it has been shown that population structure can substantially delay or prevent complete population suppression even by drives with a sufficient genetic load to reliably induce population collapse in a panmictic population (Champer et al., 2021a; North et al., 2020; North et al., 2019; Bull et al., 2019; Champer et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous spatial modeling studies.

claim: Chasing is a phenomenon where wild-type individuals recolonize regions where the drive has eliminated the population.
source: One mechanism that can prevent population collapse is 'chasing', a phenomenon where wild-type individuals recolonize regions where the drive has eliminated the population.
evidence: This is a definition of the chasing phenomenon based on modeling observations.

claim: In chasing situations, recolonizing individuals can benefit from the reduced competition due to the low population density in these areas and can substantially increase in number before the drive once again spreads into the area.
source: In this situation, the recolonizing individuals can benefit from the reduced competition due to the low population density in these areas and can substantially increase in number before the drive once again spreads into the area and causes local suppression to reoccur.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of chasing based on modeling results.

claim: Chasing is a common feature of spatial models for many types of suppression drive.
source: This chasing phenomenon seems to be a common feature of spatial models for many types of suppression drive, regardless of whether the model is implemented using abstract spatial patches (Bull et al., 2019), networks of linked demes (North et al., 2020; North et al., 2019; Birand et al., 2022), or continuous space (Champer et al., 2021a; Champer et al., 2021b; Faber et al., 2021; Liu and Champer, 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Paril and Phillips, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple spatial modeling studies.

claim: Spatial models predict that even modest differences in efficiency between drives can potentially have large effects on the outcome of a drive release.
source: Unlike panmictic models, these spatial models predict that even modest differences in efficiency between drives can potentially have large effects on the outcome of a drive release, meriting careful consideration of drive candidates to identify those with the greatest potential for success in realistic conditions.
evidence: This is based on inference from spatial modeling results.

claim: Early drives with the vasa promoter offered high germline drive conversion efficiency.
source: Early drives with the vasa promoter offered high germline drive conversion efficiency, but they are not viable candidates due to high levels of somatic Cas9 activity and high rates of embryo resistance allele formation from maternally deposited Cas9 and gRNAs (Hammond et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Vasa promoter drives are not viable candidates due to high levels of somatic Cas9 activity and high rates of embryo resistance allele formation from maternally deposited Cas9 and gRNAs.
source: Early drives with the vasa promoter offered high germline drive conversion efficiency, but they are not viable candidates due to high levels of somatic Cas9 activity and high rates of embryo resistance allele formation from maternally deposited Cas9 and gRNAs (Hammond et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Use of the zpg and nos promoters was shown to greatly reduce both embryo resistance allele formation and female fitness costs from somatic activity.
source: Use of the zpg and nos promoters was shown to greatly reduce both embryo resistance allele formation and female fitness costs from somatic activity (Hammond et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: A drive that combined the zpg promoter for Cas9 with a highly conserved gRNA target site in the dsx gene was able to successfully suppress a cage population of mosquitoes.
source: A drive that combined the zpg promoter for Cas9 with a highly conserved gRNA target site in the dsx gene (thus preventing the formation of functional resistance alleles) was able to successfully suppress a cage population of mosquitoes (Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: A highly conserved gRNA target site in the dsx gene prevents the formation of functional resistance alleles.
source: A drive that combined the zpg promoter for Cas9 with a highly conserved gRNA target site in the dsx gene (thus preventing the formation of functional resistance alleles) was able to successfully suppress a cage population of mosquitoes (Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: A follow-up study included a previously developed X-shredder in the zpg drive to create a male-biased population and was similarly successful in a cage study.
source: A follow-up study (Simoni et al., 2020) included a previously developed X-shredder in this drive (Galizi et al., 2014) to create a male-biased population and was similarly successful in a cage study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: All of the implementations of the nos drive were found to have a higher genetic load than the zpg drives.
source: All of the implementations of the nos drive were found to have a higher genetic load than the zpg drives (Figure 2), although zpg2 performed well compared to the other zpg drives.

claim: The addition of an X-shredder was detrimental to zpg2, with zpg2X's genetic load reduced by 0.16.
source: Notably, the addition of an X-shredder was detrimental to zpg2, with zpg2X's genetic load reduced by 0.16.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The addition of the X-shredder substantially improved the speed of both zpg drives.
source: The addition of the X-shredder substantially improved the speed of both zpg drives, with the zpg2 interpretation resulting in considerably higher performance than zpg.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The X-shredder was mostly present in males, allowing it to avoid somatic fitness costs in females.
source: This is because the X-shredder was mostly present in males, allowing it to avoid somatic fitness costs in females.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism explaining the improved speed.

claim: The nos drive performed far worse than all the other drives in terms of spread rate due to high fitness cost in both males and females.
source: The nos drive, with its high fitness cost in both males and females, performed far worse than all the other drives in this regard, seemingly belying its high genetic load; the somatic fitness costs had so great an impact on fertility that the drive could make little headway given a low starting frequency (though the drive still eventually reaches a high equilibrium frequency, see Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The zpg drive was unable to fully eliminate the population in spatial simulations with a low-density growth rate of 10; instead, long-term chasing occurred in 100% of simulations.
source: Under both parametrizations, the zpg drive was unable to fully eliminate the population; instead, long-term chasing occurred in 100% of simulations.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The zpg2 drive achieved suppression 28% of the time when the low-density growth rate was 10.
source: However, our alternative parameterization of the drive, zpg2, achieved suppression 28% of the time when the low-density growth rate was 10 (Figure 3A) and 63% of the time when the low-density growth rate was reduced to 6 (Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The zpg2 drive achieved suppression 63% of the time when the low-density growth rate was reduced to 6.
source: However, our alternative parameterization of the drive, zpg2, achieved suppression 28% of the time when the low-density growth rate was 10 (Figure 3A) and 63% of the time when the low-density growth rate was reduced to 6 (Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: The zpgX drive resulted in long-term chasing in almost all simulations.
source: Similar to zpg, the zpgX drive resulted in long-term chasing in almost all simulations, though the average number of fertile females was substantially reduced.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The zpg2X drive resulted in suppression in 12% of outcomes when the low-density growth rate was 10.
source: However, the alternative parametrization, zpg2X, was less likely to result in long-term chasing, and suppression was observed in 12% of outcomes when the low-density growth rate was 10 (Figure 3A) and 23% of outcomes when it was reduced to 6 (Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The zpg2X drive resulted in suppression in 23% of outcomes when the low-density growth rate was reduced to 6.
source: However, the alternative parametrization, zpg2X, was less likely to result in long-term chasing, and suppression was observed in 12% of outcomes when the low-density growth rate was 10 (Figure 3A) and 23% of outcomes when it was reduced to 6 (Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: The standard nos drive resulted in long-term chasing in almost 100% of simulations with both low-density growth rate values.
source: The standard nos drive resulted in long-term chasing in almost 100% of simulations with both low-density growth rate values (Figure 3A, Appendix 1—figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3A and Appendix 1—figure 2A.

claim: When the somatic fitness cost in heterozygote males was omitted (nosF), drive performance dramatically improved.
source: However, when the somatic fitness cost in heterozygote males was omitted (nosF), drive performance dramatically improved.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The nosF drive achieved suppression in 54% of simulations when the low-density growth rate was 10.
source: When the low-density growth rate was 10, nosF achieved suppression in 54% of simulations (Figure 3A), and when it was lowered to 6, the suppression rate increased to 89%, a notable improvement over the best performing zpg drive.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nosF drive achieved suppression in 89% of simulations when the low-density growth rate was lowered to 6.
source: When the low-density growth rate was 10, nosF achieved suppression in 54% of simulations (Figure 3A), and when it was lowered to 6, the suppression rate increased to 89%, a notable improvement over the best performing zpg drive.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With the nosF2 and nosF3 drives, suppression was almost guaranteed.
source: With a decreased female heterozygote somatic fitness cost in the nosF2 and nosF3 drive, suppression was almost guaranteed.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: Suppression tended to be increasingly likely at higher migration values and when low-density growth rates were smaller.
source: In general, suppression tended to be increasingly likely at higher migration values and when low-density growth rates were smaller (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Drive loss usually only occurred when migration values and low-density growth rates were both very low.
source: Drive loss usually only occurred when migration values and low-density growth rates were both very low (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: At higher migration values and lower growth rates, 'suppression after chasing' became more limited in duration.
source: At higher migration values and lower growth rates, 'suppression after chasing' became more limited in duration (Appendix 1—figure 7), and the average number of fertile females was reduced even during long-term chases (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: The average number of fertile females was reduced even during long-term chases at higher migration values and lower growth rates.
source: At higher migration values and lower growth rates, 'suppression after chasing' became more limited in duration (Appendix 1—figure 7), and the average number of fertile females was reduced even during long-term chases (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: A reduction in females during chasing would likely substantially reduce disease transmission.
source: Such a reduction in females would likely substantially reduce disease transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between female mosquito numbers and disease transmission.

claim: Long-term chasing outcomes were more frequent in the Anopheles-specific model than in the discrete-generation model.
source: Generally, long-term chasing outcomes were more frequent in these simulations than in the discrete-generation model (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: In the discrete-generation model with a low-density growth rate of 10, zpg2 was able to suppress the population in 28% of simulations, while the drive suppressed in only 0.5% of simulations in the mosquito model.
source: For example, in the discrete-generation model with a low-density growth rate of 10, zpg2 was able to suppress the population in 28% of simulations, while the drive suppressed in only 0.5% of simulations in the mosquito model.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: In the case of nosF, performance was decreased from suppression in 54% of simulations to only 0.5% of simulations when the low-density growth rate was set to 10 in the Anopheles-specific model.
source: In the case of nosF, performance was similarly decreased from suppression in 54% of simulations to only 0.5% of simulations when the low-density growth rate was set to 10, with the average number of fertile females during chasing increasing from 2498–4101.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: In the Anopheles-specific model, only nosF3 could reliably suppress the population in almost every simulation.
source: However, in the Anopheles-specific model, suppression often occurred only after an initial chase, and only nosF3 could reliably suppress the population in almost every simulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The zpg2X drive was able to suppress the population in 10% of simulations in the discrete-generation model, but in the Anopheles-specific model, the drive was only able to suppress 0.5% of the time.
source: The zpg2X drive also performed more poorly in this model. In the discrete-generation model, the drive was able to suppress the population in 10% of simulations, but in the Anopheles-specific model, the drive was only able to suppress 0.5% of the time.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: The reduction in the number of fertile females achieved by both X-shredder drives in the Anopheles-specific model was less pronounced and was inferior for zpg2X as compared to zpg2.
source: The reduction in the number of fertile females achieved by both X-shredder drives in this model was also less pronounced and, notably, was inferior for zpg2X as compared to zpg2.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The reduced genetic load of zpg2X outweighed the advantage of the male-bias in the Anopheles-specific model.
source: This was perhaps because the reduced genetic load of zpg2X outweighed the advantage of the male-bias.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism explaining the results.

claim: Chasing outcomes tended to replace suppression outcomes and dominate large portions of the parameter space in the Anopheles-specific model.
source: The above tendencies mostly held true in this analysis as well (see Figure 5 and Appendix 1—figures 9–14). Chasing outcomes tended to replace suppression outcomes and dominate large portions of the parameter space (Appendix 1—figures 9–11, compare with Appendix 1—figures 3–5).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in multiple figures.

claim: Drive-loss outcomes were extremely uncommon in the Anopheles-specific model compared to the discrete-generation model.
source: Drive-loss outcomes were extremely uncommon in this model compared to the discrete-generation model, with such outcomes occurring in significant quantity only when the low-density growth rate was very low (Appendix 1—figure 12, compare with Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 12 and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Only nosF2 and nosF3 performed consistently well in the Anopheles-specific model and were able to suppress the population at moderate to high migration values.
source: Only nosF2 and nosF3 performed consistently well in this model and were able to suppress the population at moderate to high migration values (Appendix 1—figure 9, compare to Appendix 1—figure 3), or at least keep the duration of chasing and average number of fertile females at low levels (Appendix 1—figures 13–14, compare to Appendix 1—figures 7–8).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in multiple figures.

claim: The drive that combined a homing drive and X-shredder may be less capable of suppressing a population than the original dsx drive with the zpg promoter alone, particularly in a spatially continuous population.
source: In this study, we analyzed several possible types of homing gene drives for population suppression of the malaria vector Anopheles gambiae. Various parameter sets for each of these drives were considered, representing alternative explanations for fertility measurements previously conducted (Simoni et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018; Hammond et al., 2021). We found that the drive that combined a homing drive and X-shredder may actually be less capable of suppressing a population than the original dsx drive with the zpg promoter alone, particularly in a spatially continuous population.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and analysis.

claim: The nos promoter may be a preferable alternative for Cas9 expression compared to the zpg promoter, depending on which interpretation of the experimental data proves to be the most accurate.
source: Further, we found that the nos promoter may be a preferable alternative for Cas9 expression compared to the zpg promoter, depending on which interpretation of the experimental data proves to be the most accurate.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and analysis.

claim: The rate of paternal Cas9 deposition for a given Cas9 promoter could be assessed using a split-drive system.
source: For example, the rate of paternal Cas9 deposition for a given Cas9 promoter could be assessed using a split-drive system (Champer et al., 2019), sequencing, or conducting a fertility assessment of offspring that have a drive-carrier father but that do not themselves inherit a drive allele.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental work based on established methods.

claim: Batch effects could have a large impact on fertility measurements.
source: Batch effects could also have a large impact on fertility measurements (Hammond et al., 2021), which we have also noticed in our Drosophila experiments (Champer et al., 2020c; Champer et al., 2020a; Metzloff et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A combined X-shredder system may not represent an improvement to the standard homing suppression drive.
source: Based on our modeling results, it appears that a combined X-shredder system may not represent an improvement to the standard homing suppression drive for a couple of reasons.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation results.

claim: With the alternate parameter set, the genetic load of the combined X-shredder drive is lower and is perhaps not high enough to reliably suppress a robust wild population.
source: First, with the alternate parameter set, the genetic load of this drive is lower (even with perfect homing, the 93% shredding rate would yield a genetic load of only 0.87) and is perhaps not high enough to reliably suppress a robust wild population.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and inference.

claim: X-shredders fundamentally induce lower genetic load than female fertility homing drives when at the same germline efficiency.
source: X-shredders fundamentally induce lower genetic load than female fertility homing drives when at the same germline efficiency, and a combined system can be expected to generally have the characteristics and genetic load of an X-shredder rather than a homing suppression drive, at least when the X-shredding efficiency is fairly high.
evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding of drive mechanisms.

claim: The drives including the X-shredder do not seem to perform well in spatial simulations, even with higher shredding rates due to drive wave dynamics and stochastic factors at high drive frequency.
source: Second, the drives including the X-shredder do not seem to perform well in spatial simulations, even with higher shredding rates due to drive wave dynamics and stochastic factors at high drive frequency (Champer et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is based on simulation results and citation to previous work.

claim: Combined X-shredder systems can provide a way to support some continued suppression even in the presence of functional resistance alleles.
source: However, combined X-shredder systems are not without advantages. They can provide a way to support some continued suppression even in the presence of functional resistance alleles (although the rate that such alleles form at dsx is unknown and may already be sufficiently low due to the highly conserved nature of the target site, which is essential at the sequence level Champer et al., 2021a, and it could likely be further reduced by the use of a drive with multiplexed gRNAs Champer et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding and citations.

claim: X-shredders bias the population toward males, which may effectively reduce biting females more quickly than standard homing suppression drives.
source: Also, because X-shredders bias the population toward males, such systems may effectively reduce biting females (and therefore reduce disease transmission) more quickly than standard homing suppression drives (Simoni et al., 2020), although female dsx drive homozygotes also cannot bite (Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on inference and citations to previous work.

claim: Female dsx drive homozygotes cannot bite.
source: Also, because X-shredders bias the population toward males, such systems may effectively reduce biting females (and therefore reduce disease transmission) more quickly than standard homing suppression drives (Simoni et al., 2020), although female dsx drive homozygotes also cannot bite (Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The original zpg interpretation does not perform well due to paternal mosaic Cas9 deposition.
source: Among the other drives we considered, the original zpg interpretation does not perform well due to paternal mosaic Cas9 deposition.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and analysis.

claim: Paternal mosaic Cas9 deposition tends to greatly reduce genetic load because at high frequencies, female drive carriers more often inherit their drive allele from a male drive parent because female homozygotes are also sterile.
source: This tends to greatly reduce genetic load because at high frequencies, female drive carriers (who suffer from paternal deposition) more often inherit their drive allele from a male drive parent because female homozygotes are also sterile.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism explaining the reduced genetic load.

claim: The high rate of paternal deposition used to parameterize the original zpg variant is not likely to be an accurate interpretation of the data, especially considering the excellent performance of this drive in cage populations.
source: Fortunately, the high rate of paternal deposition used to parameterize this variant is not likely to be an accurate interpretation of the data, especially considering the excellent performance of this drive in cage populations (Kyrou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with experimental results.

claim: The increased performance of nos drives presumably comes from the reduction of somatic fitness costs between nos, nosF, nosF2, and nosF3.
source: Between the nos drives, the increased performance presumably comes from the reduction of somatic fitness costs between nos, nosF, nosF2, and nosF3.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism explaining performance differences.

claim: Reduction of somatic fitness costs does not affect the ultimate genetic load, but it substantially affects the rate that these drives increase in frequency.
source: Though this does not affect the ultimate genetic load, it substantially affects the rate that these drives increase in frequency.
evidence: This is based on simulation results and inference.

claim: In a spatial scenario, faster drive increase allows the drive to more rapidly convert wild-type alleles into drive alleles, reducing the opportunities for a chasing dynamic to emerge.
source: In a spatial scenario, this factor allows the drive to more rapidly convert wild-type alleles into drive alleles, reducing the opportunities for a chasing dynamic to emerge, and allowing the drive to catch up more quickly if chasing does occur.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism explaining spatial performance.

claim: The results of the Anopheles-specific continuous space model mirror the outcomes of the earlier generic model of suppression gene drives in continuous space, but the drives have substantially greater difficulty eliminating the population.
source: In general, the results of our Anopheles-specific continuous space model mirror the outcomes of our earlier generic model (Champer et al., 2021a) of suppression gene drives in continuous space, but the drives have substantially greater difficulty eliminating the population.
evidence: This is based on comparison of simulation results between models.

claim: In the Anopheles-specific model, chasing outcomes were substantially more common, suggesting that chasing may be difficult to avoid when using a gene drive in natural populations unless the drive meets stringent efficiency criteria.
source: Indeed, in the Anopheles-specific model, chasing outcomes were substantially more common, suggesting that chasing may be difficult to avoid when using a gene drive in natural populations unless the drive meets stringent efficiency criteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation results.

claim: Differences between models were likely at least partially due to the fact that competition in the Anopheles model affects offspring viability rather than female fecundity.
source: These differences between models were likely at least partially due to the fact that competition in the Anopheles model affects offspring viability rather than female fecundity.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism explaining model differences.

claim: Fertile Anopheles individuals are not inhibited in reproduction due to competition by sterile individuals, as opposed to fertile females in the discrete-generation model.

Specifically, we believe that a standard homing suppression drive using the nos promoter (Carballar-Lejarazú et al., 2020; Hammond et al., 2021) for Cas9 (possibly a high fidelity variant to avoid off-target cleavage Langmüller et al., 2022) and targeting dsx (Simoni et al., 2020; Kyrou et al., 2018) with two or more closely spaced gRNA target sites (Yang et al., 2022; Champer et al., 2020b) may be the optimal combination of currently available tools for population suppression of Anopheles mosquitoes.
